======================================================================
ARTICLE: Frying
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{short description|Cooking food in oil or fat}}
[[File:PLAINTAIN.jpg|thumb|alt=Slices of plantain being fried in a wide pan outside in bubbling oil|[[Fried plantain]]|218x218px]]
'''Frying''' is a method of [[cooking]] where food is made in [[cooking oil|oil]] or [[animal fat]].<ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Artisan Books| isbn = 978-1-57965-236-4| last = Peterson| first = James| title = Essentials of Cooking| date = April 2003}}</ref> Frying is believed to have first appeared in Ancient Egypt around 2500 BC, with tiger nut cakes deep fried in oil.<ref name=":5" /> 

A variety of foods can be fried. The amount of oil or fat will usually affect the food's taste and texture. Foods fried in more oil, or [[Deep frying|deep fried]], will typically be crispier or more tender,<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Valente |first=Lisa |title=Air-Frying vs. Deep-Frying: How They Compare in Calories, Fat, and Flavor. |url=https://www.foodandwine.com/air-frying-health-breakdown-11929996}}</ref> whereas foods fried in less oil, like [[shallow frying]] or [[pan frying]], will usually still be crisp but to a lesser extent. Other methods utilize the movement of the food in the pan or using oil or fat with other sauces.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=What's the healthiest way to cook vegetables? |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/food/articles/healthiest_vegetable_cooking_method |access-date=2026-10-09 |website=BBC Food |language=en-GB}}</ref> 

Frying is a [[Dehydration reaction|dehydration process]] which involves the transfer of mass and heat. Different chemical changes take place during the frying process such as [[protein denaturation]], [[starch gelatinization]], surface browning, rapid water evaporation and oil absorption.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Onigbogi |first1=Isaac O |last2=Olatunji |first2=T.O |last3=Nupo |first3=S.S |last4=Bello |first4=T.K |date=December 2011 |title=Effect of Repeated Frying Operations on the Quality Attributes of Frying Oil and Acceptability of Sweet Potato Chips |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/304898163 |journal=Journal of Sciences and Multidisciplinary Research |volume=3 |pages=10 |via=ResearchGate}}</ref>

==History==
Frying is believed to have first appeared in [[Ancient Egyptian cuisine]] during the [[Old Kingdom of Egypt|Old Kingdom]], around 2500 BC.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last=Quiles |first=Joules L. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ebwx5iZIJI8C&dq=frying+ancient+egypt&pg=PA74 |title=Olive Oil and Health |date=2006 |publisher=CABI |isbn=978-1-84593-072-1 |language=en}}</ref> Ancient Egyptians would typically fry foods like tiger nut cakes, [[fish]], and other foods.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parode |first=Nancy |date=2024-10-22 |title=The Origin Of Deep Fried Food Traces Back To Ancient Egypt |url=https://www.tastingtable.com/1691693/ancient-history-of-deep-fried-food/ |access-date=2026-10-08 |website=Tasting Table |language=en-US}}</ref> In the tomb of Egyptian [[Vizier]] [[Rekhmire]], who lived in the 15th century BC,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rekhmire |url=https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q650643 |access-date=2026-10-09 |website=www.wikidata.org |language=en}}</ref> there are depictions of workers putting small cakes in pots of oil or fat and instructions in [[Egyptian hieroglyphs|hieroglyphics]] to fry the food.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Five foods the ancient Egyptians used to eat |url=https://www.middleeasteye.net/discover/egypt-ancient-five-foods-eaten |access-date=2026-10-09 |work=Middle East Eye |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Nina de Garis Davies - Cooking Cakes with Fat, Tomb of Rekhmire - New Kingdom - The Metropolitan Museum of Art |url=https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/544623 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260309183436/https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/544623 |archive-date=2026-03-09 |access-date=2026-10-08 |website=www.metmuseum.org |language=en}}</ref>

During the [[Warring States period]] of the [[Zhou dynasty]] (475-221 BC), the [[Rites of Zhou]] and the [[Book of Rites]] were written and contained information and recipes about the eight delicacies. The eight delicacies are recipes and culinary techniques. One of the eight delicacies is chun ao. Chun means to enrich, and ao means to fry.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Clements |first=Jonathan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7wQxEAAAQBAJ&dq=chun+ao+book+of+rites&pg=PT49 |title=The Emperor's Feast: 'A tasty portrait of a nation' –Sunday Telegraph |date=2021-02-11 |publisher=Hodder & Stoughton |isbn=978-1-5293-3243-8 |language=en}}</ref> Chun ao is fried, pickled meat paste poured on top of [[upland rice]] mixed with rendered animal fat.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mather |first=Richard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c6mgEAAAQBAJ&dq=chun+ao+food&pg=PA332 |title=The Age of Eternal Brilliance: Three Lyric Poets of the Yung-ming Era (483-493) Vol. I |date=2022-11-28 |publisher=BRILL |isbn=978-90-04-53176-5 |language=en}}</ref>

In the late 2nd century AD, Greek cook [[Galen]] describes [[pancake]]-like griddle cakes made with [[sesame seeds]] and fried in olive oil over a fire.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Linden |first=Grace |title=A Brief History of Pancakes |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/a-brief-history-of-pancakes-180981667/ |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Cook a classical feast: nine recipes from ancient Greece and Rome {{!}} British Museum |url=https://www.britishmuseum.org/blog/cook-classical-feast-nine-recipes-ancient-greece-and-rome |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=www.britishmuseum.org |language=en}}</ref> Later, in the 5th century AD, the Roman cookbook [[Apicius]] describes a Delian sweet from the Greek island [[Delos]]. The dessert is made with hardened wheat paste that is then deep fried in oil.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Museum |first=Hellenic |date=2021-08-12 |title=Sweet Treats |url=https://www.hellenic.org.au/post/sweet-treats |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=Hellenic Museum |language=en}}</ref> Commonly, the Delian sweets are covered in honey and pepper before being served.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" />

== Process ==
When in contact with oil heated to {{convert|150|{{ndash}}|200|C}}, food undergoes heat and mass transfer.<ref name="Changes in food" /> The food's [[water content]] reaches [[boiling point]] and begins to [[vaporise|vaporize]], creating pores in its [[cell walls]] which enable it to absorb oil.<ref name="Food Safety and Health">{{cite journal |last1=Valle |first1=Consuelo |last2=Echeverría |first2=Francisca |last3=Chávez |first3=Vilma |last4=Valenzuela |first4=Rodrigo |last5=Bustamante |first5=Andrés |title=Deep-frying impact on food and oil chemical composition: Strategies to reduce oil absorption in the final product |journal=Food Safety and Health |date=2024 |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=414–428 |doi=10.1002/fsh3.12056 |doi-access=free }}</ref> As heat exposure is greater on the surface of the food in direct contact with the oil, water vaporization occurs more quickly. This dehydration effect causes a crisp crust to form which protects the center of the food against further oil absorption.<ref name="Food Safety and Health" />

The crust browns due to the formation of [[melanoidins]] caused by [[caramelization]] and the [[Maillard reaction]]. The food's starch content [[Starch gelatinization|gelatinizes]], causing it to soften; the surface contains less water and retains its crisp crust.<ref name="Changes in food">{{cite journal |last1=Bordin |first1=Keliani |last2=Tomihe Kunitake |first2=Mariana |last3=Kazue Aracava |first3=Keila |last4=Silvia Favaro Trindade |first4=Carmen |title=Changes in food caused by deep fat frying |journal=Órgano Oficial de la Sociedad Latinoamericana de Nutrición |date=2013 |volume=63 |issue=1 |url=https://ve.scielo.org/scielo.php?script=sci_abstract&pid=S0004-06222013000100001&lng=es&nrm=iso&tlng=en |access-date=5 May 2026 |issn=0004-0622}}</ref> Frying is complete when all water content in the food vaporizes.<ref name="Food Safety and Health" /> When a fried food reduces in temperature below {{convert|100|C|F}}, water vapor inside condenses and internal pressure drops, causing oil absorption into the food via a vacuum effect.<ref name="Food Safety and Health" />

== Techniques ==
=== Air frying ===
{{Main|Convection oven}}In air frying, food is placed in an air fryer with a small amount of oil and then heated to an extreme temperature.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Ray |first=Joe |date=2018-05-10 |title=Are Air Fryers Worth It? |url=https://www.wired.com/story/air-fryers/ |access-date=2026-10-09 |magazine=Wired |language=en-US |issn=1059-1028}}</ref> Air fryers are typically considered to be a healthier alternative to frying, as they usually have less [[Calorie|calories]] and a lower fat content than deep fried or shallow fried foods.<ref name=":2" />[[File:Munkinpaisto.jpg|thumb|193x193px|alt=Rings of dough floating in bubbling oil, varying in colour from cream to dark brown|[[Smultring]] being deep fried]]

=== Deep frying ===
{{Main|Deep frying}}
In deep frying, food is submerged in hot [[Cooking oil|oil]] or [[fat]] so that all sides are cooked simultaneously. A [[deep fryer]] or [[chip pan]] may be used, or, in an industrial frying operation, a [[pressure fryer]] or [[vacuum fryer]]. One method for preparing food for deep frying involves [[Batter (cooking)|battering]] or [[breading]], which adds color and crunch to its surface.<ref name="Food prep NVQ2">{{cite book |last1=Stevenson |first1=Danny |title=Food Preparation and Cooking: Cookery Units |date=1996 |publisher=Nelson Thornes Ltd |isbn=0-7487-2566-0 |page=18 |edition=2nd |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vRcidxIUWYMC&pg=PA18 |access-date=4 May 2026}}</ref> [[French fries]], [[doughnuts]], [[cong you bing]], and [[tempura]] are common deep-fried foods.<ref name="Oxford Companion"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Y. W. Ang |first1=Catharina |last2=Liu |first2=KeShun |last3=Huang |first3=Yao-Wen |title=Asian Foods: Science and Technology |date=1999 |publisher=Technomic Publishing Company, Inc. |isbn=1-56676-736-9 |page=94 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C4cTXJYTE4QC&pg=PA94 |access-date=4 May 2026}}</ref>
=== Sautéing ===
{{Main|Sautéing}}
In sautéing, food is tossed over high heat in a [[frying pan]] with a small amount oil to prevent sticking.<ref name="Frying Fats Boskou">{{cite book |last1=Boskou |first1=Dimitrios |title=Frying Fats |date=2011 |publisher=CRC Press |edition=2 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/259575170 |access-date=10 May 2026}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> A shallow pan or sauté pan are what is typically used for sautéing foods.<ref name="Oxford Companion">{{cite book |last1=Davidson |first1=Alan |title=The Oxford Companion to Food |date=1999 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=0192115790 |url=https://archive.org/details/oxfordcompaniont0000davi_g3y4/mode/2up |access-date=11 May 2026}}</ref> Sauté pans usually have higher sides to prevent food from exiting the pan while tossing.

=== Shallow frying ===
{{Main|Shallow frying}}
In shallow frying, also known as pan frying, food is partially submerged and fried in shallow oil on one side until browned, then flipped to cook the other side.<ref name="Oxford Companion"/>[[File:Wok cooking.jpg|225px|thumb|right|A [[wok]] being used to stir fry]]

=== Stir frying ===
{{Main|Stir frying}}

Stir frying is a [[Chinese cuisine|Chinese]], high-heat technique using a [[wok]] in which ingredients are constantly stirred for even cooking. The base of the wok is placed directly in the fire and its concave shape allows the flames to envelop the bowl; the base of the wok can reach {{convert|400|C|F}}.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lam |first1=Lan |title=The Science of Stir-Frying in a Wok |url=https://www.americastestkitchen.com/articles/2189-the-science-of-stir-frying-in-a-wok |website=America's Test Kitchen |date=April 2020 |access-date=7 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="Chinese cooking">{{cite book |last1=Lo |first1=Eileen Yin-Fei |title=Mastering the Art of Chinese Cooking |date=2009 |publisher=Chronicle Books LLC |isbn=978-0811859332 |page=76}}</ref> Frying is finished in two to three minutes.<ref name="Chinese Cooking (1945)">{{cite book |last1=Chao |first1=Yang Buwei |title=How to Cook and Eat in Chinese |date=1945 |publisher=The John Day Company |url=https://archive.org/details/howtocookeatinch00cha0/mode/2up |access-date=7 May 2026}}</ref>
== Health effects ==
A 2021 [[meta-analysis]] found that the highest category of fried food consumption compared to the lowest is associated with a 3% increase in the risk of all-cause [[Mortality rate|mortality]], as well as with a 2% increase in the risk of [[cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular]] mortality.<ref name=qin-mortality>{{cite journal |vauthors=Qin P, Zhang M, Han M, Liu D, Luo X, Xu L, Zeng Y, Chen Q, Wang T, Chen X, Zhou Q, Li Q, Qie R, Wu X, Li Y, Zhang Y, Wu Y, Hu D, Hu F |title=Fried-food consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of observational studies |journal=Heart |volume=107 |issue=19 |pages=1567–1575 |date=October 2021 |pmid=33468573 |doi=10.1136/heartjnl-2020-317883 |url=}}</ref> Compared to participants with a low intake, those who ate the most fried food had a 37% increased risk of [[heart failure]], a 28% increased risk of major cardiovascular events, and a 22% increased risk of [[coronary heart disease]].<ref name=qin-mortality /> The risk of [[stroke]], heart failure, and [[Myocardial infarction|heart attack]] modestly increased with the increase of weekly servings of fried food.<ref name=qin-mortality /> The study concluded that fried food consumption may increase the risk of cardiovascular disease and presents a linear [[dose–response relationship|dose-response relation]].<ref name=qin-mortality /> The researchers theorized the main reasons behind these associations are the high trans fat and calorie content of fried foods and their [[pro-inflammatory]] nature.<ref name=qin-mortality /> It was also noted that eating [[hyperpalatable]] crisp-fried foods may entice people to engage in routine overeating.<ref name=qin-mortality />

A 2023 meta-analysis found that fried food consumption is linked to a 52% increase in the risk of [[stomach cancer]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Zhang T, Song SS, Liu M, Park S |title=Association of Fried Food Intake with Gastric Cancer Risk: A Systemic Review and Meta-Analysis of Case-Control Studies |journal=Nutrients |volume=15 |issue=13 |date=June 2023 |page=2982 |pmid=37447308 |pmc=10347084 |doi=10.3390/nu15132982 |doi-access=free |url=}}</ref> Fried food intake is also associated with [[prehypertension]],<ref name=provido>{{cite journal |vauthors=Provido SM, Abris GP, Hong S, Yu SH, Lee CB, Lee JE |title=Association of fried food intake with prehypertension and hypertension: the Filipino women's diet and health study |journal=Nutr Res Pract |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=76–84 |date=February 2020 |pmid=32042377 |pmc=6997139 |doi=10.4162/nrp.2020.14.1.76 |url=}}</ref> [[hypertension]]<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Sayon-Orea C, Bes-Rastrollo M, Gea A, Zazpe I, Basterra-Gortari FJ, Martinez-Gonzalez MA |title=Reported fried food consumption and the incidence of hypertension in a Mediterranean cohort: the SUN (Seguimiento Universidad de Navarra) project |journal=Br J Nutr |volume=112 |issue=6 |pages=984–91 |date=September 2014 |pmid=25201306 |doi=10.1017/S0007114514001755 |url=}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Kang Y, Kim J |title=Association between fried food consumption and hypertension in Korean adults |journal=Br J Nutr |volume=115 |issue=1 |pages=87–94 |date=January 2016 |pmid=26449129 |doi=10.1017/S000711451500402X |url=}}</ref><ref name=provido /><ref name=qin-diseases>{{cite journal |vauthors=Qin P, Liu D, Wu X, Zeng Y, Sun X, Zhang Y, Li Y, Wu Y, Han M, Qie R, Huang S, Zhao Y, Feng Y, Yang X, Liu Y, Li H, Zhang M, Hu D, Hu F |title=Fried-food consumption and risk of overweight/obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension in adults: a meta-analysis of observational studies |journal=Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr |volume=62 |issue=24 |pages=6809–6820 |date=2022 |pmid=33825582 |doi=10.1080/10408398.2021.1906626 |url=}}</ref> and [[obesity]].<ref name=qin-diseases /><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Guallar-Castillón P, Rodríguez-Artalejo F, Fornés NS, Banegas JR, Etxezarreta PA, Ardanaz E, Barricarte A, Chirlaque MD, Iraeta MD, Larrañaga NL, Losada A, Mendez M, Martínez C, Quirós JR, Navarro C, Jakszyn P, Sánchez MJ, Tormo MJ, González CA |title=Intake of fried foods is associated with obesity in the cohort of Spanish adults from the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition |journal=Am J Clin Nutr |volume=86 |issue=1 |pages=198–205 |date=July 2007 |pmid=17616781 |doi=10.1093/ajcn/86.1.198 |url=|doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Nutrition ===
Due to oil absorption during frying, the nutritional profile of the oil used becomes part of the final product; up to 75% of calories can be from fat in fried foods.<ref name="Changes in food" /> 15% of [[Batter (cooking)|battered]] chicken or fish’s final weight is absorbed frying oil, compared to 20% when [[Breading|breaded]]. [[Doughnuts]]’ final weight is between 15{{ndash}}20% frying oil, and this figure increases to up to 35{{ndash}}40% for [[potato chips]].<ref name="Industrial Frying">{{cite journal |last1=Rosseli |first1=J. B. |title=Industrial Frying Process |journal=Grasas y Aceites |date=30 August 1998 |volume=49 |issue=3–4 |pages=282–295 |doi=10.3989/gya.1998.v49.i3-4.729|url=https://grasasyaceites.revistas.csic.es/index.php/grasasyaceites/article/view/729 |access-date=3 April 2026|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Vitamins like [[thiamin]], [[riboflavin]], and [[vitamin A]] are unstable at high temperatures and [[vitamin C]] is [[water soluble]], meaning they can be lost from fried foods during water evaporation. Vitamin A is particularly unstable{{mdash}}24% of vitamin A is destroyed during frying compared to 14% when [[boiled]] due to [[oxidation]]. [[Fiber]] increases in fried foods due to the formation of brown [[melanoidins]], which form part of the crust. The proportion of [[protein]] also increases due to the concentrating effects of dehydration, with the exception of amino acid [[lysine]] due to its role in the [[Maillard reaction]]. [[Minerals]] increase in concentration in the same way, but this means that [[heavy metals]] found in some fish are also concentrated during frying.<ref name="Changes in food" />

=== Fume inhalation ===
Toxic compounds such as aldehydes (e.g. [[formaldehyde]]) are produced during frying and evaporate with steam, which can irritate lung tissue if inhaled.<ref name="Frying Fats Boskou"/> Fumes from frying have been classified as "probably carcinogenic to humans" by the [[International Agency for Research on Cancer]].<ref name="Food Veg Oils">{{cite journal |last1=Abrante-Pascual |first1=Susana |last2=Nieva-Echevarría |first2=Barbara |last3=Goicoechea-Oses |first3=Encarnacion |title=Vegetable Oils and Their Use for Frying: A Review of Their Compositional Differences and Degradation |journal=Foods |date=23 December 2024 |volume=13 |issue=24 |pages=4186 |doi=10.3390/foods13244186 |doi-access=free |pmid=39767128 |pmc=11675685 }}</ref>

== Effects of oil ==
During frying, oil is exposed to water from food, high temperatures, and oxygen from the surroundings, which cause degradation. [[Hydrolysis]] causes an oil's smoke point to decrease and [[oxidation]] causes the formation of volatile compounds which change the flavor, quality, and texture of the food.<ref name="Chemistry of Oils"</> These are mostly toxic [[aldehydes]], of which some amount is required to achieve a characteristic fried smell and taste.<ref name="Changes in food" /> Oils have varying proportions of [[Saturated fat|saturated]], [[monounsaturated]], and [[polyunsaturated]] fats which change their performance during frying.<ref name="Chemistry of Oils">{{cite journal |last1=Choe |first1=E. |last2=Min |first2=D. B. |title=Chemistry of Deep-Fat Frying Oils |journal=Journal of Food Science |date=1 May 2007 |volume=72 |issue=5 |pages=R77-86 |doi=10.1111/j.1750-3841.2007.00352.x |pmid=17995742 |url=https://ift.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1750-3841.2007.00352.x |access-date=13 May 2026|url-access=subscription |via=IFT}}</ref>

=== Monounsaturated fats ===

[[Rapeseed oil]], also known as canola oil, is the third most used frying oil, especially in northern Europe, Japan, Oceania, and Canada. Despite mostly comprising [[monounsaturated fat]], its high [[linolenic acid]] content makes it prone to oxidation. [[Peanut oil]], also known as groundnut oil, is commonly used in west Africa but, unlike rapeseed oil, is low in linolenic acid.<ref name="Chemistry of Oils"</> [[Olive oil]] is stable at high temperatures because of its high monounsaturated fat and [[antioxidant]] content, which make it less likely to oxidize during frying and improves the nutritional content of fried foods.<ref name="Food Safety and Health" /> It degrades two times as slowly as [[sunflower oil]] and ten times as slowly as [[linseed oil]]. Its widespread use may be the cause of fried food consumption not being linked to increased [[mortality rate|mortality]] in Mediterranean countries.<ref name="Chemistry of Oils"</>

=== Polyunsaturated fats ===
Polyunsaturated fats are most prone to [[oxidation]] and [[polymerization]], which form toxic compounds that are absorbed by food.<ref name="Chemistry of Oils"</> A 2022 [[WHO]] review and meta-analysis of 170 studies found that [[polyunsaturated fat]] consumption reduced overall mortality, but that higher quality evidence was needed.<ref>{{cite book |last1=J. de Souza |first1=Russell |last2=A. Zulyniak |first2=Michael |last3=Kazemi |first3=Mina |last4=Ali |first4=Rahim |last5=Bierbrier |first5=Rachel |last6=Williams |first6=Natalie |last7=Stennett |first7=Rosain |last8=Banfield |first8=Laura |title=Polyunsaturated fatty acids intake and risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, mental health, and type 2 diabetes |date=2022 |publisher=World Health Organisation |isbn=978-92-4-006164-4 |url=https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/18dccfe5-6d1a-426c-a99a-29b664ee371e/content |access-date=6 May 2026}}</ref> [[Sunflower oil]] is most commonly used in eastern Europe. Despite being a source of vitamin E, its high polysaturated fat content makes it poor for frying. Sunflower oil is sold with added [[oleic acid]] to increase its monounsaturated fat content and therefore its stability.<ref name="Chemistry of Oils"</>

=== Saturated fats ===

[[Palm oil]] is the most common oil, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, southeast Asia, and some parts of South America. Its saturated and unsaturated fat content are nearly equal, but is slightly more saturated. It has a high [[palmitic acid]] content, which is linked to [[heart disease]].<ref name="Chemistry of Oils"</>

=== Oil reuse ===
Oil is reused in industrial frying to reduce costs, but prolonged use causes [[oxidation]], producing [[aldehydes]] that affect flavor and increase [[cancer]] risks.<ref name="Food Safety and Health" /> Unsaturated fats oxidize more quickly than saturated fats, and oils with high linolenic acid content can result fish-like smell.<ref name="Changes in food" /><ref name="Chemistry of Oils"</> Oil reuse reduces the nutritional value of foods and increases saturated and [[trans fats]] while reducing monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats.<ref name="Food Safety and Health" /> Foods fried in reused oil absorb more.<ref name="Changes in food" />

=== Fire risks ===
Oil or fat with a [[smoke point]] below {{convert|200|C|F}} may foam and rise, spilling and causing a fire. Foaming can be distinguished from bubbles caused by water evaporation because the foam covers the whole surface of the oil, not just above the food.<ref name="Industrial Frying" /> Blended oils are more prone to foaming.<ref name="Frying Fats Boskou" /> Oil with a [[flash point]] below {{convert|315|C|F}} may explode.<ref name="Industrial Frying" />

======================================================================
ARTICLE: Gastronomy
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{short description|Study of the relationship between food and culture}}
{{more footnotes|date=June 2016|reason=Some of these are probably not even appropriate sources.}}
[[Image:Produits régionaux - photo CPPR.jpg|thumb|200px|Fine food, the principal study of gastronomy]]
'''Gastronomy''' is the study of the relationship between [[Human food|food]] and [[culture]], the art of preparing and serving rich or delicate and appetizing food, the cooking styles of particular regions, and the science of good eating.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-11 |title=Gastronomy {{!}} Description, History, & Cuisine {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/gastronomy |access-date=2023-06-27 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref> One who is well versed in gastronomy is called a '''gastronome''', while a '''gastronomist''' is one who unites theory and practice in the study of gastronomy. Practical gastronomy is associated with the practice and study of the preparation, production, and service of the various foods and beverages, from countries around the world. It is related with a system and process approach, focused on recipes, techniques and cookery books. Food gastronomy is connected with food and beverages and their genesis. Technical gastronomy underpins practical gastronomy, introducing a rigorous approach to evaluation of gastronomic topics.<ref name="GillespieCousins2012">{{cite book |first1=Cailein |last1=Gillespie |first2=John |last2=Cousins |title=European Gastronomy into the 21st Century |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=2G5cihKVlOIC |date=23 May 2012 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-1-136-40493-1 |page=4}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=Crystal |last=Cun |title=What the Hell Is Gastronomy, Anyway? |work=Adventures of an Omnomnomnivore<!--not a typo--> in NYC |publisher=self-published |date=13 May 2011 |url= https://www.crystal.kitchen/2011/05/13/what-the-hell-is-gastronomy-anyway |access-date=7 August 2020}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The word ''gastronomy'' originates from the title of a poem quoted by the ancient Greek rhetorician [[Athenaeus]]. It is a compound of Greek {{lang|grc|γαστρ(ο)-}} {{transliteration|grc|gastr(o)-}} (from {{lang|grc|γαστήρ}} {{transliteration|grc|gastḗr}}, {{gloss|stomach}}) and {{lang|grc|νόμος}} {{transliteration|grc|nómos}} ({{gloss|custom}}), modeled on ''astronomy''.<ref>{{cite dictionary|date=1898 |title=gastronomy, n. |url=https://www.oed.com/dictionary/gastronomy_n |url-access=subscription |dictionary=[[Oxford English Dictionary]] |location=[[Oxford]] |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |access-date=11 August 2025}}</ref> The term was revived in 1801 as the title of a poem by {{ill|Joseph Berchoux|fr}},<ref name="Ory1996pp445-448">{{cite book |last=Ory |first=Pascal |title=Realms of Memory: Tradition |date=1996 |publisher=[[Columbia University Press]] |pages=445–448}}</ref><ref>Joseph Berchoux, ''La gastronomie, pöeme'', 4th edition, Paris, 1805 [https://books.google.com/books?id=FXIEUS3gHrUC full text]</ref> though it was [[Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin]] in his ''Physiologie du goût'' (1825) who systematized the study of food and cooking under this name.<ref>Béa Aaronson, "La Civilisation du goût: Savoir et saveur à la table de Louis XIV", in ''Civilization in French and Francophone Literature'', ''French Literature Series'' '''33''' (2006), p. 88</ref>

== History ==
Gastronomy involves discovering, tasting, experiencing, researching, understanding and writing about food preparation and the sensory qualities of [[human nutrition]] as a whole. It also studies how nutrition interfaces with the broader culture. The biological and chemical basis of cooking has become known as [[molecular gastronomy]], while gastronomy covers a much broader, interdisciplinary ground. {{citation needed|date=June 2025}}

[[File:Jean François Tourcaty, Carte Gastronomique de la France, 1809 Cornell CUL PJM 1033 01.jpg|thumbnail|This is the first example of a carte gastronomique, a map that summarizes a country by its products at the outset of the  "Cours Gastronomique" by Charles Louis Cadet de Gassicourt (1809).]]
Pascal Ory, a French historian, defines gastronomy as the establishment of rules of eating and drinking, an "art of the table", and distinguishes it from good cooking ({{lang|fr|bonne cuisine}}) or fine cooking ({{lang|fr|[[haute cuisine]]}}). Ory traces the origins of gastronomy back to the French reign of [[Louis XIV]] when people took interest in developing rules to discriminate between good and bad style and extended their thinking to define good culinary taste. The lavish and sophisticated cuisine and practices of the French court became the culinary model for the French. [[Alexandre Balthazar Laurent Grimod de La Reynière|Alexandre Grimod de La Reynière]] wrote the gastronomic work {{lang|fr|[[Almanach des Gourmands]]}} (1803), elevating the status of food discourse to a disciplined level based on his views of French tradition and morals. Grimod aimed to reestablish order lost after the revolution and institute gastronomy as a serious subject in France. Grimod expanded gastronomic literature to the three forms of the genre: the guidebook, the gastronomic treatise, and the gourmet periodical. The invention of gastronomic literature coincided with important cultural transformations in France that increased the relevance of the subject. The end of nobility in France changed how people consumed food; fewer wealthy households employed cooks and the new bourgeoisie class wanted to assert their status by consuming elitist food. The emergence of the restaurant satisfied these social needs and provided good food available for popular consumption. The center of culinary excellence in France shifted from Versailles to Paris, a city with a competitive and innovative culinary culture. The culinary commentary of Grimod and other gastronomes influenced the tastes and expectations of consumers in an unprecedented manner as a third party to the consumer-chef interaction.<ref name="Ory1996pp445-448" />

The French origins of gastronomy explain the widespread use of French terminology in gastronomic literature. Pascal Ory criticizes this literature as conceptually vague; relying heavily on anecdotal evidence; and using confusing, poorly defined terminology. Nevertheless, gastronomy has grown from a marginalized subject in France to a serious and popular interest worldwide.<ref name="Ory1996pp445-448" />

The derivative ''[[gourmet]]'' has come into use since the publication of ''Physiology of Taste'' ({{lang|fr|Physiologie du goût}}) an 1825 cooking treatise by [[Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin]], a lawyer and politician who aimed to define classic [[French cuisine]]. While the work contains some flamboyant recipes, it goes into the theory of preparation of French dishes and hospitality.{{sfnp|Brillat-Savarin|2004}} According to Brillat-Savarin: "Gastronomy is the knowledge and understanding of all that relates to man as he eats. Its purpose is to ensure the conservation of men, using the best food possible."{{sfnp|Brillat-Savarin|2004}}<ref>{{cite book |last=Montagné |first=Prosper |title=[[Larousse gastronomique]] |edition=2nd English ("New American") |editor-first=Jennifer |editor-last=Harvey Lang |location=New York |publisher=Crown |date=1988 |orig-year=1938}} The translation of the Brillat-Savarin quotation is from this work.</ref>

==Writings on gastronomy==
Many writings on gastronomy throughout the world capture the thoughts and aesthetics of a culture's cuisine during a period in their history. Some works continue to define or influence the contemporary gastronomic thought and cuisine of their respective cultures.

Some additional historical examples:
*{{lang|la|[[Apicius]]}} or {{lang|la|De re Coquinaria}} (''On the Subject of Cooking''): A 1st-to-5th-century collection of [[Ancient Rome|ancient Roman]] recipes, often attributed (without clear evidence) to the gourmet [[Marcus Gavius Apicius]], it contains instructions for preparing [[Ancient Roman cuisine|dishes]] enjoyed by the elite of the time. A new English translation was published in 2009 as ''Cookery and Dining in Imperial Rome''.{{sfnp|Apicius|2009}}
*{{lang|zh-Latn|[[Suiyuan Shidan]]}} ({{lang|zh|隨園食單}}, ''The Way of Eating'', also known in English as ''Recipes from the Garden of Contentment''): An 18th-century manual on [[Chinese cuisine]] of [[Qing dynasty]] by the poet [[Yuan Mei]], it contains recipes from different social classes at the time along with two chapters on Chinese gastronomic and culinary theory. The first translation into English was completed in 2017.{{sfnp|Yuan|2017}}

ARTICLE: Herb
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT

{{short description|Plant used for food, medicine or perfume}}
{{about|culinary, medicinal, and spiritual herbs|the people|Herb (given name)|and|Herb (surname)|the botanical usage|herbaceous plant|other uses}}
[[File:Garden of herbs.jpg|thumb|A variety of herbs are visible in this [[garden]], including [[Mentha|mint]] and [[parsley]].]]

'''Herbs'''<!--please do not change to the singular; this has caused problems over "an herb" vs. "a herb"--> are a widely distributed and widespread group of plants, excluding [[vegetables]], with savory or aromatic properties that are used for flavoring and [[garnish (food)|garnishing]] food, for medicinal purposes, or for fragrances. Culinary use typically distinguishes herbs from [[spices]]. ''Herbs'' generally refers to the [[leaf]]y green or [[flower]]ing parts of a plant (either fresh or dried), while ''spices'' are usually dried and produced from other parts of the plant, including [[seed]]s, [[Bark (botany)|bark]], [[root]]s and [[fruit]]s.

Herbs have a variety of uses including culinary, medicinal, aromatic and in some cases, spiritual. General usage of the term "herb" differs between culinary herbs and [[medicinal herb]]s; in medicinal or spiritual use, any parts of the plant might be considered "herbs", including leaves, roots, flowers, seeds, root bark, inner bark (and [[Vascular cambium|cambium]]), [[resin]] and [[pericarp]].

The word "herb" is pronounced {{IPAc-en|h|ɜːr|b}} in [[Commonwealth English]],<ref>{{cite book |title=Cambridge Advanced Learners' Dictionary & Thesaurus |publisher=Cambridge University Press |chapter=Herb |chapter-url=https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/british/herb?q=herb}}</ref> but {{IPAc-en|ɜːr|b}} is standard among [[American English]] speakers as well as those from regions where [[h-dropping]] occurs. In [[Canadian English]], both pronunciations are common.<ref>{{cite web |title='H' an ingredient of modern herb |date=12 October 2009 |url=https://www.thestar.com/life/2009/10/12/h_an_ingredient_of_modern_herb.html |publisher=Toronto Star |access-date=2 June 2023}}</ref> In botany, the noun "herb" refers to a "plant that does not produce a woody stem", and the adjective "herbaceous" means "herb-like", referring to parts of the plant that are "green and soft in texture".<ref name="Carolin">{{cite book |last1=Carolin |first1=Roger C. |last2=Tindale |first2=Mary D. |title=Flora of the Sydney region |date=1994 |publisher=Reed |location=Chatswood, NSW |isbn=0730104001 |page=23 |edition=4th}}</ref><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |title=Glossary of Botanical Terms |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&glossary=yes&alpha=F-H |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=8 March 2021}}</ref>
{{Quote box
 |quote="What is a herb?" "The friend of physicians and the praise of cooks."
 |author = --[[Alcuin]] and his student [[Charlemagne]]<ref name="Freeman" />
 |width  = 25%
 |align  = right
}}

==Definition==
[[File:The Herb Garden - geograph.org.uk - 1629279.jpg|thumb|Herb garden at [[Hardwick Hall]], [[Derbyshire]], [[England]], originally planted in the 1870s by Lady Louisa Egerton, recreated by the [[National Trust]], largely following the original design.]]
In [[botany]], the term herb refers to a [[herbaceous plant]],<ref name="RHS encyclopedia">{{cite book |title=The Royal Horticultural Society encyclopedia of gardening |year=2004 |publisher=Dorling Kindersley |isbn=9781405303538 |edition=2nd |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pulnPwAACAAJ|pages=404, 679}}</ref> defined as a small, [[Spermatophyte|seed-bearing plant]] without a woody stem in which all aerial parts (i.e. above ground) die back to the ground at the end of each [[growing season]].<ref name="Allaby2012">{{cite book |last1=Allaby |first1=Michael |title=A Dictionary of Plant Sciences |date=2012 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780191079030 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DB09DAAAQBAJ}}</ref> Usually the term refers to [[Perennial plant|perennials]],<ref name="RHS encyclopedia" /> although herbaceous plants can also be [[Annual plant|annuals]] (plants that die at the end of the growing season and grow back from seed next year),<ref name="Stuart1989">{{cite book |last1=Stuart |first1=Malcolm |title=The Encyclopedia of herbs and herbalism |date=1989 |publisher=Crescent Books |isbn=978-0517353264 |page=7}}</ref> or [[Biennial plant|biennial]]s.<ref name="RHS encyclopedia" /> This term is in contrast to [[shrub]]s and [[tree]]s which possess a woody stem.<ref name="Allaby2012" /> Shrubs and trees are also defined in terms of size, where shrubs are less than ten meters tall, and trees may grow over ten meters.<ref name="Allaby2012" /> The word herbaceous is derived from Latin ''herbāceus'' meaning "grassy", from ''herba'' "grass, herb".<ref name="OED">{{cite book |title=Oxford dictionary of English. |date=2010 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780199571123 |page=819 |edition=3rd |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=anecAQAAQBAJ}}</ref>

Another sense of the term herb can refer to a much larger range of plants,<ref name="Bown1995">{{cite book |last1=Bown |first1=Deni |title=Encyclopedia of herbs & their uses |url=https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofhe00bown |url-access=registration |date=1995 |publisher=Dorling Kindersley |isbn=978-0751302035 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofhe00bown/page/10 10], 11}}</ref> with culinary, therapeutic or other uses.<ref name="RHS encyclopedia" /> For example, some of the most commonly described herbs such as [[Salvia|sage]], [[rosemary]] and [[Lavandula|lavender]] would be excluded from the botanical definition of an herb as they do not die down each year, and they possess woody stems.<ref name="Stuart1989" /> In the wider sense, herbs may be herbaceous perennials but also trees, subshrubs, shrubs, annuals, [[liana]]s, [[fern]]s, [[moss]]es, [[algae]],<ref name="Bown1995" /> [[lichen]]s, and [[fungi]].<ref name="Stuart1989" /> [[Herbalism]] can utilize not just stems and leaves but also fruit, roots, bark and gums.<ref name="Stuart1989" /> Therefore, one suggested definition of an herb is a plant which is of use to humans,<ref name="Stuart1989" /> although this definition is problematic since it could cover a great many plants that are not commonly described as herbs.

== History ==
Ancient Greek philosopher [[Theophrastus]] divided the plant world into trees, shrubs, and herbs.<ref name="Bremness1994">{{cite book |last1=Bremness |first1=Lesley |title=The complete book of herbs |year=1994 |publisher=Viking Studio Books |isbn=9780140238020 |page=8 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VqfnrH-W2kwC}}</ref> The [[Talmud]], a foundational Jewish text from antiquity, references approximately fifteen different herbs used for seasoning.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Broshi |first=Magen |title=Bread, Wine, Walls and Scrolls |date=2001 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing PLC |isbn=978-1-84127-201-6 |series=The Library of Second Temple Studies |location=London |pages=138}}</ref> Herbs came to be considered in three groups, namely [[pot herb]]s (e.g. onions), sweet herbs (e.g. thyme), and salad herbs (e.g. wild celery).<ref name="Stuart1989" /> During the seventeenth century, as [[selective breeding]] changed the plants' size and flavor away from the wild plant, pot herbs began to be referred to as [[vegetable]]s as they were no longer considered only suitable for the pot.<ref name="Stuart1989" />

Botany and the study of herbs were, in their infancy, primarily a study of the pharmacological uses of plants. During the Middle Ages, when [[humoral theory]] guided medicine, it was posited that foodstuffs, possessing their own humoral qualities, could alter the humoral temperaments of people. Parsley and sage were often used together in medieval cookery, for example in [[chicken broth]], which had developed a reputation as a therapeutic food by the 14th century. One of the most common sauces of the age, [[green sauce]], was made with parsley and often sage as well. In a 14th-century recipe recorded in [[Latin]] "for lords, for settling their temperament and whetting their appetite" green sauce is served with a dish of cheese and whole egg yolks boiled in watered down wine with herbs and spices.<ref>
{{cite book |title=Health and Healing From the Medieval Garden |date=2008 |publisher=The Boydell Press |isbn=9781843833635 |page=67}}</ref>

== Reproduction ==
[[Perennial herbs]] are usually reproduced by stem cuttings, either softwood cuttings of immature growth, or hardwood cuttings where the bark has been scraped to expose the [[cambium]] layer. A cutting is usually approximately {{convert|3|to|4|in|cm|0}} in length. Plant roots can grow from the stems. Leaves are stripped from the lower portion up to one half before the cutting is placed in growth medium or rooted in a glass of water. This process requires high humidity in the environment, sufficient light, and root zone heat.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Tucker |first1=Arthur |last2=Debaggio |first2=Thomas |title=The Encyclopedia of Herbs |publisher=Timber Press |location=London}}</ref>

== Uses ==
=== Culinary ===
{{See also|List of culinary herbs and spices}}
[[File:Thyme-Bundle.jpg|thumb|A bundle of [[Thymus (plant)|thyme (''Thymus'')]]]]
Culinary herbs are distinguished from [[vegetable]]s in that, like spices, they are used in small amounts and provide [[Flavor (taste)|flavor]] rather than substance to [[food]].<ref name="Small National Research Council Canada 2006">{{cite book |last=Small |first=E. |author2=National Research Council Canada |title=Culinary Herbs |publisher=NRC Research Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-660-19073-0 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UL9lpNrx0kwC&pg=PA1 |access-date=9 October 2018 |page=1}}</ref>

Herbs can be perennials such as [[thyme]], [[oregano]], [[Salvia officinalis|sage]] or [[lavender]], biennials such as [[parsley]], or annuals like [[basil]]. Perennial herbs can be shrubs such as rosemary (''Rosmarinus officinalis''), or trees such as [[bay laurel]] (''Laurus nobilis'') – this contrasts with [[Herbaceous plant|botanical herbs]], which by definition cannot be woody plants. Some plants are used as both herbs and spices, such as [[dill]] weed and dill seed or [[coriander]] leaves and seeds. There are also some herbs, such as those in the [[Lamiaceae|mint family]], that are used for both culinary and medicinal purposes.

Emperor [[Charlemagne]] (742–814) compiled a list of 74 different herbs that were to be planted in his gardens. The connection between herbs and health is important already in the European Middle Ages--''[[The Forme of Cury]]'' (that is, "cookery") promotes extensive use of herbs, including in salads, and claims in its preface "the assent and advisement of the masters of physic and philosophy in the King's Court".<ref name="Freeman">{{cite book |title=Herbs for the Medieval Household, for Cooking, Healing and Divers uses |pages=ix–x |first=Margaret B. |last=Freeman |location=New York |publisher=The Metropolitan Museum of Art |year=1943}}</ref>

=== Teas ===
{{main|Herbal tea}}
Some herbs can be infused in boiling water to make [[herbal tea]]s (also termed tisanes).<ref name="RHS encyclopedia" /><ref name="Bown1995" /> Typically the dried leaves, flowers or seeds are used, or fresh herbs are used.<ref name="RHS encyclopedia" /> Herbal teas tend to be made from aromatic herbs,<ref name="Bremness1994" /> may not contain [[tannin]]s or [[caffeine]],<ref name="RHS encyclopedia" /> and are not typically mixed with milk.<ref name="Bown1995" /> Common examples include [[chamomile tea]],<ref name="Bown1995" /> or [[mint herbal tea|mint tea]].<ref name="Bremness1994" /> Herbal teas are often used as a source of relaxation or can be associated with rituals.<ref name="Bremness1994" />

=== Medicine  ===
{{Main|Medicinal plants|Herbalism}}
{{see also|List of plants used in herbalism|}}
[[File:Chinese herbal decoction (一貫煎) on snow.jpg |thumb|right|alt= An image of decocted Chinese medicine 一貫煎 on snow, taken in the United States. The snow is on the border of a forest near a residential area, with a small lake in the background near trees. |
A traditional Chinese decoction (湯劑/汤剂), using [[Chinese herbology|Chinese herbs]]]]
[[File:In Effigiam Nicholai Culpeper Equitis by Richard Gaywood.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Nicholas Culpeper]] was an English [[botany|botanist]], [[Herbalism|herbalist]], [[physician]], and [[astrology|astrologer]].<ref name="ODNB">Patrick Curry: "Culpeper, Nicholas (1616–1654)", ''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'' (Oxford, UK: OUP, 2004)</ref> (etching by Richard Gaywood between 1644 and 1662)]]

Herbs were used in [[prehistoric medicine]]. As far back as 5000 BCE, evidence that [[Sumer]]ians used herbs in medicine was inscribed on cuneiform.<ref>{{cite book |first=Ruth D. |last=Wrensch |title=The Essence of Herbs |publisher=University Press of Mississippi |year=1992 |page=9}}</ref> In 162 CE, the physician [[Galen]] was known for concocting complicated herbal remedies that contained up to 100 ingredients.<ref name="Tapsell">{{cite journal |vauthors=Tapsell LC, Hemphill I, Cobiac L, Sullivan DR, Fenech M, Patch CS, Roodenrys S, Keogh JB, Clifton PM, Williams PG, Fazio VA, Inge KE |date=2006 |title=Health benefits of herbs and spices: The past, the present, the future |journal=Medical Journal of Australia |volume=185 |issue=4 |pages=S1–S24 |doi=10.5694/j.1326-5377.2006.tb00548.x |pmid=17022438 |s2cid=9769230 |url=http://ro.uow.edu.au/hbspapers/1397/|hdl=2440/22802 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

Some plants contain [[phytochemical]]s that have effects on the body. There may be some effects when consumed in the small levels that typify culinary "spicing", and some herbs are toxic in larger quantities. For instance, some types of herbal extract, such as the extract of St. John's-wort (''[[Hypericum perforatum]]'') or of kava (''[[Piper methysticum]]'') can be used for medical purposes to relieve depression and stress.<ref>{{cite book |author=Adele G Dawson |title=Herbs, Partners in Life: Healing, Gardening and Cooking with Wild Plants |publisher=Bear & Co. |year=2000 |pages=5–6}}</ref> However, large amounts of these herbs may lead to toxic overload that may involve complications, some of a serious nature, and should be used with caution. Complications can also arise when taken with some prescription medicines.

Herbs have long been used as the basis of traditional [[Chinese herbal medicine]], with usage dating as far back as the first century [[Common Era|CE]] and far before. In India, the [[Ayurveda]] medicinal system is based on herbs. Medicinal use of herbs in Western cultures has its roots in the [[Hippocratic]] (Greek) elemental healing system, based on a quaternary elemental healing metaphor. Famous herbalist of the Western tradition include [[Avicenna]] (Persian), [[Galen]] (Roman), [[Paracelsus]] (German Swiss), [[Nicholas Culpeper|Culpepper]] (English) and the botanically inclined Eclectic physicians of 19th century/early 20th century America ([[John Milton Scudder]], [[Harvey Wickes Felter]], [[John Uri Lloyd]]). Modern pharmaceuticals had their origins in crude herbal medicines, and to this day, some drugs are still extracted as fractionate/isolate compounds from raw herbs and then purified to meet pharmaceutical standards.

There is a record dated 1226 for '12d for Roses for Baron's Chamber and in 1516 for flowers and rushes for chambers for Henry the 9th<ref name="RHS encyclopedia" />

Certain herbs contain psychoactive properties that have been used for both religious and recreational purposes by humans since the early [[Holocene]] era, notably the leaves and extracts of the [[cannabis]] and [[coca]] plants. The leaves of the coca plant have been chewed by people in northern [[Peru]]vian societies for over 8,000 years,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Dillehay T, Rossen J, Ugent D, Karathanasis A, Vásquez V, Netherly P |year=2010 |title=Early Holocene coca chewing in northern Peru |journal=Antiquity |volume=84 |issue=326 |pages=939–953 |doi=10.1017/S0003598X00067004|s2cid=162889680 }}</ref> while the use of cannabis as a psychoactive substance dates back to the first century CE in [[China]] and northern [[Africa]].<ref>{{cite book |author=Ernest Abel |title=Marihuana: The First Twelve Thousand Years |publisher=Springer |location=New York |year=1980 |isbn=978-0-306-40496-2 |url=https://cannabis-truth.yolasite.com/resources/Abel.%20marihuana%20the%20first%20twelve%20thousand%20years.pdf |access-date=2018-07-25}}</ref>

[[Indigenous Australian]] peoples developed "[[bush medicine]]" based on plants that were readily available to them. The isolation of these groups meant the remedies developed were for far less serious diseases than the western illnesses they contracted during colonisation. Herbs such as [[Mentha australis|river mint]], [[Acacia pycnantha|wattle]] and [[eucalyptus]] were used for coughs, diarrhea, fever and headaches.<ref name="Tapsell" />

=== Ritual ===
{{Main|Sacred herb}}
[[File:Balsamodendron ehrenbergianum00.jpg|thumb|upright|''[[Commiphora gileadensis]]'' (Gilead myrrh)]]
Herbs are used in many [[religion]]s. During the monastic era, monks would cultivate herbs alongside vegetables, while others would be set aside in a [[physic garden]] for specific purposes.<ref>{{cite book |title=English Herb Garden |first1=Guy |last1=Cooper |first2=Gordon I. |last2=Taylor |publisher=Random House |year=1986}}</ref> For example, [[myrrh]] (''Commiphora myrrha'') and [[frankincense]] (''Boswellia'' species) in [[Hellenistic religion]], the [[Nine Herbs Charm|nine herbs charm]] in [[Anglo-Saxon paganism]], [[neem]] (''Azadirachta indica'') leaves, [[Aegle marmelos|bael]] (''Aegele marmelos'') leaves, holy basil or ''tulsi'' (''[[Ocimum tenuiflorum]]''), [[turmeric]] or "haldi" (''Curcuma longa''), [[cannabis]] in [[Hinduism]], and [[white sage]] in [[Wicca]]. [[Rastafari movement|Rastafari]] also consider [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]] to be a holy plant.

[[Siberia]]n [[shaman]]s also used herbs for spiritual purposes. Plants may be used to induce spiritual experiences for rites of passage, such as [[vision quest]]s in some [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native American]] cultures. The [[Cherokee]] use both [[Salvia apiana|white sage]] and [[Cedar wood|cedar]] for spiritual cleansing and [[Smudge stick|smudging]].

=== Cosmetics ===
Originally, there was always doubt in ancient societies, especially in the sceptical medium of western traditions, as to the efficacy of herbal medicines. The use of [[herbal cosmetics]] dates back around six centuries ago in Europe and Western countries. Mixtures and pastes were often concocted to whiten the face. During the 1940s, herbal cosmetics took a turn with the emerging red lipstick color, with every year gaining a more intense red. Herbal cosmetics come in many forms, such as face creams, scrubs, lipstick, natural fragrances, powders, body oils, deodorants and sunscreens. They activate through the epithelium of sebaceous glands to make the skin more supple. Ayurvedic oils are widely used in India, prized for their natural health-giving properties.<ref>{{cite book |first=H. |last=Panda |title=Herbal Cosmetics Handbook |edition=3rd |publisher=Asia-Pacific Business Press |year=2015}}</ref>

One method and perhaps the best,{{cn|date=July 2026}} used to extract natural oils from herbs to make lipstick is [[partition chromatography]]. The process involves separation in a watery solution, and then the injection of colour under pressure.

=== Other  ===
{{main|Strewing herb}}
Strewing herbs are scattered (strewn) over the floors of dwelling places and other buildings. Such plants usually have fragrant or astringent smells, and many also serve as [[insecticide]]s (e.g. to repel fleas) or disinfectants. For example, [[Filipendula ulmaria|meadowsweet]] (''Filipendula ulmaria'') was sometimes strewn across floors in the Middle Ages because of its sweet smell.<ref name="Bown1995" />

======================================================================
ARTICLE: Maillard reaction
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{Short description|Chemical reaction that gives browned food flavor}}
[[File:Brioche.jpg|right|thumb|The crusts of most [[bread]]s, such as this [[brioche]], are golden-brown mostly as a result of the Maillard reaction.]]

The '''Maillard reaction''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|m|aɪ|j|ɑr|(|d|)}} {{respell|MY|ar(d)}}; {{IPA|fr|majaʁ|lang}}) is a [[chemical reaction]] between [[amino acid]]s and [[reducing sugar]]s to create [[melanoidin]]s, the compounds that give browned food its distinctive flavor. [[Searing|Seared]] steaks, fried dumplings, cookies and other kinds of biscuits, breads, toasted marshmallows, falafel and many other foods undergo this reaction. It is named after French chemist [[Louis Camille Maillard]], who first described it in 1912 while attempting to reproduce [[Protein biosynthesis| biological protein synthesis]].<ref name="maillard_1912">{{cite journal| last =Maillard |first = L. C. |author-link=Louis Camille Maillard| date = 1912
| title = Action des acides amines sur les sucres; formation de melanoidines par voie méthodique| trans-title=Action of amino acids on sugars. Formation of melanoidins in a methodical way | journal = [[Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences|Comptes Rendus]]| volume = 154| pages = 66–68| url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=umn.31951d00015504w&view=1up&seq=74 |language=fr }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Chichester |editor-first=C. O. |title=Advances in Food Research |volume=30 |series=Advances in Food and Nutrition Research |publisher=Academic Press |location=Boston |date=1986 |isbn=0-12-016430-2 |page=79}}</ref> The reaction is a form of [[Food browning|non-enzymatic browning]] which typically proceeds rapidly from around {{convert|140|to|165|C|round=10}}. Many [[recipe]]s call for an oven temperature high enough to ensure that a Maillard reaction occurs.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Bui|first1=Andrew|title=Why So Many Recipes Call for a 350-Degree Oven|url=https://www.tastingtable.com/cook/national/why-bake-350-degrees|website=Tasting Table|access-date=6 November 2017|date=2017-09-29}}</ref> At higher temperatures, [[caramelization]] (the browning of sugars, a distinct process) and subsequently [[pyrolysis]] (final breakdown leading to burning and the development of acrid flavors) become more pronounced.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-09-06|title=Here's How to Sear a Steak to Perfection|url=https://homecookworld.com/how-to-sear-a-steak/|access-date=2022-01-27|website=Home Cook World|language=en|archive-date=2022-01-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220127085525/https://homecookworld.com/how-to-sear-a-steak/}}</ref>

The reactive [[carbonyl group]] of the sugar reacts with the [[Nucleophile|nucleophilic]] [[amine|amino group]] of the amino acid and forms a complex mixture of poorly characterized molecules responsible for a range of aromas and flavors. This process is accelerated in an alkaline environment (e.g., [[lye]] applied to darken pretzels; see [[lye roll]]), as the amino groups ({{chem2|RNH3+->RNH2}}) are [[Deprotonation|deprotonated]], and hence have an increased [[Nucleophile|nucleophilicity]]. This reaction is the basis for many of the [[flavoring]] industry's recipes. At high temperatures, a probable<ref name="tamanna" /> [[carcinogen]] called [[acrylamide]] can form.<ref name="tareke">{{cite journal |last1=Tareke |first1=E. |last2=Rydberg |first2=P. |last3=Karlsson |first3=Patrik |last4=Eriksson |first4=Sune |last5=Törnqvist |first5=Margareta |date=2002 |title=Analysis of acrylamide, a carcinogen formed in heated foodstuffs |journal=J. Agric. Food Chem. |pmid=12166997 |doi=10.1021/jf020302f|volume=50 |issue=17 |pages=4998–5006}}</ref> This can be discouraged by heating at a lower temperature, adding [[asparaginase]], or injecting carbon dioxide.<ref name="tamanna">{{cite journal |last1=Tamanna |first1=N |last2=Mahmood |first2=N |title=Food Processing and Maillard Reaction Products: Effect on Human Health and Nutrition. |journal=International Journal of Food Science |date=2015 |volume=2015 |article-number=526762 |doi=10.1155/2015/526762 |pmid=26904661 |pmc=4745522 |issn=2314-5765|doi-access=free }}</ref>

In the cooking process, Maillard reactions can produce hundreds of different flavor compounds depending on the chemical constituents in the food, the temperature, the cooking time, and the presence of air. These compounds, in turn, often break down to form yet more flavor compounds. Flavorists have used the Maillard reaction over the years to make artificial flavors, the majority of patents being related to the production of meat-like flavors.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Danehy |first1=James P. |editor1-last=Chicester |editor1-first=C.O. |title=Maillard Reactions: Nonenzymatic Browning in Food Systems with Special Reference to the Development of Flavor |journal=Advances in Food Research |date=May 19, 1986 |volume=30 |page=107 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0065262808603481/pdf?md5=d9319f7f0fa089bc3d64af3d0e714ad4&pid=1-s2.0-S0065262808603481-main.pdf |access-date=15 March 2024 |publisher=Academic Press|doi=10.1016/s0065-2628(08)60348-1 |pmid=3526830 |isbn=978-0-12-016430-1 }}</ref> According to chemistry Nobel Prize winner [[Jean-Marie Lehn]] "The Maillard is, by far, the most widely practiced chemical reaction in the world".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Everts |first=Sarah |date=2025-01-21 |title=The Maillard Reaction Turns 100 |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/90/i40/Maillard-Reaction-Turns-100.html |access-date=2025-08-20 |website=Chemical & Engineering News |language=en}}</ref>

== History ==
In 1912, [[Louis Camille Maillard]] published a paper describing the reaction between [[amino acid]]s and sugars at elevated temperatures.<ref name="maillard_1912" /> In 1953, chemist [[John E. Hodge]] with the [[United States Department of Agriculture|U.S. Department of Agriculture]] established a mechanism for the Maillard reaction.<ref name="hodge_1953">{{cite journal| last = Hodge |first=J. E.| date = 1953| title = Dehydrated Foods, Chemistry of Browning Reactions in Model Systems| journal = Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry| volume = 1 |issue=15| pages=928–43 |doi=10.1021/jf60015a004
}}</ref><ref name="everts_2012">{{cite journal| last= Everts |first=Sarah| date = October 1, 2012| title = The Maillard Reaction Turns 100| journal = Chemical & Engineering News| volume = 90| issue=40| pages = 58–60| url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/90/i40/Maillard-Reaction-Turns-100.html|doi=10.1021/cen-09040-scitech2| url-access= subscription}}</ref>

== Foods and products ==
[[File:6-Acetyl-2,3,4,5-tetrahydropyridine.svg|thumb|200px|6-Acetyl-2,3,4,5-tetrahydropyridine]]
[[File:2-Acetyl-1-pyrroline.svg|thumb|200px|2-Acetylpyrroline]]

The Maillard reaction is responsible for many colors and flavors in foods, such as the [[Browning (partial cooking)|browning]] of various meats when seared or grilled, the browning and [[umami]] taste in [[fried onion]]s and [[coffee roasting]]. It contributes to the darkened crust of [[baking|baked goods]], the golden-brown color of [[French fries]] and other [[crisps]], browning of [[malted barley]] as found in [[malt]] whiskey and beer, and the color and taste of [[Powdered milk|dried]] and [[condensed milk]], ''[[dulce de leche]]'', [[black garlic]], [[chocolate]], [[Marshmallow#Toasted marshmallows|toasted marshmallows]], and [[peanut#Dry-roasted peanuts|roasted peanuts]].{{Citation needed|date=February 2021}}

[[6-Acetyl-2,3,4,5-tetrahydropyridine]] is responsible for the biscuit or cracker-like flavor present in baked goods such as bread, popcorn, and tortilla products. The structurally related compound [[2-Acetyl-1-pyrroline|2-acetyl-1-pyrroline]] has a similar smell and also occurs naturally without heating. The compound gives varieties of cooked rice and the herb ''pandan'' (''[[Pandanus amaryllifolius]]'') their typical smells. Both compounds have [[Odor detection threshold|odor thresholds]] below 0.06 nanograms per liter.<ref>{{cite journal| last1=Harrison |first1 = T. J. |last2=v |first2=G. R. | date = 2005| title = An expeditious, high-yielding construction of the food aroma compounds 6-acetyl-1,2,3,4-tetrahydropyridine and 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline| journal = [[J. Org. Chem.]]| volume = 70| issue = 26| pages = 10872–74| pmid = 16356012| doi = 10.1021/jo051940a}}</ref>
[[File:Schweinsbraten-1.jpg|thumb|Roast pork, browned using the Maillard reaction]]
[[File:fries 2.jpg|thumb|The preparation of French fries at high temperature can lead to the formation of [[acrylamide]].<ref name=tareke />]]

The browning reactions that occur when meat is roasted or seared are complex and occur mostly by Maillard browning<ref name=McGee2004>{{cite book |last=McGee |first=Harold |date=2004 |title=On Food and Cooking: The Science and Lore of the Kitchen |isbn=978-0-684-80001-1 |publisher=Scribner |location=New York |pages=778–79}}</ref> with contributions from other chemical reactions, including the breakdown of the [[tetrapyrrole]] rings of the muscle protein [[myoglobin]]. Maillard reactions also occur in [[dried fruit]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Miranda |first1=Gonzalo |last2=Berna |first2=Angel |last3=Mulet |first3=Antonio |title=Dried-Fruit Storage: An Analysis of Package Headspace Atmosphere Changes |journal=Foods |date=4 February 2019 |volume=8 |issue=2 |page=56 |doi=10.3390/foods8020056 |pmid=30720722 |pmc=6406843 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and when [[champagne]] ages in the bottle.<ref>
{{cite book |last=Liem |first=Peter |date=2017 |title=Champagne: The Essential Guide to the Wines, Producers, and Terroirs of the Iconic Region |isbn=978-1-78472-447-4 |publisher=Ten Speed Press |page=66}}</ref>

[[Caramelization]] is an entirely different process from Maillard browning, though the results of the two processes are sometimes similar to the naked eye (and taste buds). Caramelization may sometimes cause browning in the same foods in which the Maillard reaction occurs, but the two processes are distinct. They are both promoted by heating, but the Maillard reaction involves amino acids, whereas caramelization is the [[pyrolysis]] of certain sugars.<ref name="wp-maillard2020">{{Cite news |last=Krystal |first=Becky |date=2020-01-31 |title=The Maillard reaction: What it is and why it matters |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/voraciously/wp/2020/01/31/the-maillard-reaction-what-it-is-and-why-it-matters/ |access-date=2022-07-28 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

In the production of animal feed, the Maillard reaction can reduce feed quality by reducing the digestibility of amino acids.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lopez |first=Diego A |last2=Stein |first2=Hans H |last3=Miesner |first3=Matt D |last4=Gebhardt |first4=Jordan T |last5=Stark |first5=Charles R |last6=Paulk |first6=Chad B |date=2025-01-07 |title=Effect of feed conditioning time prior to pelleting on standardized ileal digestibility of amino acids and total tract digestibility of energy in diets fed to growing pigs |url=https://academic.oup.com/tas/article/doi/10.1093/tas/txaf153/8317558 |journal=Translational Animal Science |language=en |volume=9 |doi=10.1093/tas/txaf153 |issn=2573-2102|doi-access=free }}</ref> In making [[silage]], excess heat causes the Maillard reaction to occur, which reduces the amount of energy and protein available to the animals that feed on it.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cooper |first1=Phil |title=Grass Silage Stability and Maillard Silage |url=https://www.fcgagric.com/2017/05/02/grass-silage-stability-and-maillard-silage/ |website=Farm Consultancy |access-date=2 August 2022 |language=en |date=2 May 2017}}</ref>

== Archaeology and paleontology ==
In archaeology, the Maillard process occurs when bodies are preserved in [[Bog|peat bog]]s. The acidic peat environment causes a [[Tanning (leather)|tanning]] or browning of skin tones and can turn hair to a red or ginger tone. The chemical mechanism is the same as in the browning of food, but it develops slowly over time due to the acidic action on the [[bog body]]. It is typically seen on [[Iron Age]] bodies and is the result of the interaction of anaerobic, acidic, and cold (typically {{cvt|4|°C}}) sphagnum acid on the [[polysaccharide]]s.

The Maillard reaction also contributes to the preservation of [[paleofeces]].<ref>{{cite web
 |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/hard-core-sequencing |title=Hard-core sequencing |last=Dove |first=Alan |date=11 February 2016 |website=Science |publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science |access-date=16 June 2021 |quote=In a dry environment, the Maillard reaction—the same chemical process that browns a steak—causes feces to develop a protective outer shell.}}</ref>

== Chemical mechanism ==
# The [[carbonyl group]] of the sugar reacts with the amino group of the amino acid, producing N-substituted [[glycosylamine]] and water
# The unstable glycosylamine undergoes [[Amadori rearrangement]], forming [[ketosamine]]s
# Several ways are known  for the ketosamines to react further:
#* Produce two water molecules and [[reductone]]s
#* [[Diacetyl]], [[pyruvaldehyde]], and other short-chain [[hydrolytic]] fission products can be formed.
#* Produce brown nitrogenous polymers and [[melanoidin]]s

[[File:Maillard.svg|Mechanism of formation of Amadori product from D-glucose]]
<!-- Might want to check the structure of the "Schiff base" You have 5 bonds to nitrogen...-->

The open-chain [[Amadori rearrangement|Amadori]] products undergo further dehydration and deamination to produce dicarbonyls.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1039/9781847552570-00005 |chapter=The Chemistry of Nonenzymic Browning |title=The Maillard Reaction |year=2007 |last1=Nursten |first1=Harry |pages=5–30 |isbn=978-0-85404-964-6 }}</ref>
This is a crucial intermediate.

[[File:Dicarbonyls-correction.png|Formation of [[dicarbonyl]] from open-chain Amadori compound]]

Dicarbonyls react with amines to produce Strecker aldehydes through [[Strecker degradation]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stadler |first1=Richard H. |last2=Robert |first2=Fabien |last3=Riediker |first3=Sonja |last4=Varga |first4=Natalia |last5=Davidek |first5=Tomas |last6=Devaud |first6=Stéphanie |last7=Goldmann |first7=Till |last8=Hau |first8=Jörg |last9=Blank |first9=Imre |title=In-Depth Mechanistic Study on the Formation of Acrylamide and Other Vinylogous Compounds by the Maillard Reaction |journal=Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry |date=August 2004 |volume=52 |issue=17 |pages=5550–5558 |doi=10.1021/jf0495486 |pmid=15315399 }}</ref>

[[Acrylamide]], a possible human [[carcinogen]],<ref>[https://www.cancer.org/cancer/risk-prevention/chemicals/acrylamide.html Acrylamide]. Cancer.org. Retrieved on 2024-12-27.</ref> can be generated as a byproduct of the Maillard reaction between reducing sugars and amino acids, especially [[asparagine]], both of which are present in most food products.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Virk-Baker |first1=Mandeep K. |last2=Nagy |first2=Tim R. |last3=Barnes |first3=Stephen |last4=Groopman |first4=John |title=Dietary Acrylamide and Human Cancer: A Systematic Review of Literature |journal=Nutrition and Cancer |date=29 May 2014 |volume=66 |issue=5 |pages=774–790 |doi=10.1080/01635581.2014.916323 |pmid=24875401 |pmc=4164905 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mottram |first1=Donald S. |last2=Wedzicha |first2=Bronislaw L. |last3=Dodson |first3=Andrew T. |title=Acrylamide is formed in the Maillard reaction |journal=Nature |date=October 2002 |volume=419 |issue=6906 |pages=448–449 |doi=10.1038/419448a |pmid=12368844 |bibcode=2002Natur.419..448M |s2cid=4360610 }}</ref>
